entities.summary:
Thomas Murner (c. 1475 – 1537) was an Alsatian Franciscan friar, prolific satirist, poet, and polemicist whose venomous wit made him one of the most vociferous literary opponents of the Protestant Reformation in the early 16th century. Born in Oberehnheim, within the Holy Roman Empire, Murner studied at various European universities, including Freiburg, Paris, and Krakow, before his ordination in 1494. His significance lies in his vigorous defense of Catholic doctrine through vernacular literature, engaging directly with the theological and social upheavals initiated by Martin Luther and other reformers, thereby shaping the intellectual battlegrounds of the era.

Murner's literary career was marked by a series of influential satirical works, notably *Narrenbeschwörung* (The Conjuration of Fools, 1512) and *Schelmenzunft* (The Guild of Rogues, 1512), which employed the popular genre of *Narrenliteratur* to critique societal vices and human folly. As the Reformation gained momentum, his focus shifted to direct polemic against Luther, producing works like *Von dem grossen Lutherischen Narren* (Of the Great Lutheran Fool, 1522), a biting personal attack designed to discredit the reformer through caricature and accusation. Beyond satire, Murner was also a translator, completing the first full German translation of Virgil's *Aeneid* in 1515, demonstrating his diverse literary talents and commitment to enriching German vernacular literature.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Thomas Murner was a pivotal figure in the literary and theological battles of the early German Reformation, his prolific and biting satires providing a significant Catholic counter-voice to Protestant reformers. His works influenced the character of religious polemic and contributed to the development of early modern German vernacular literature.
